note: Verdicts from the fan-out's own critics - one per scheme, fresh context, none grading its own build. Recorded so tools/collect-schemes.mjs can honour them: a scheme its critic REJECTED is NOT adopted, however well-formed its geometry is. Structural validity is necessary and not sufficient - a scheme can pass every geometric check and still fail to embody the operation it was built to test.

S7-WATER.name: THE CATCH
S7-WATER.critic:
PARTLY — the surplus is real, the sizing logic is not, and the machine has no geometry.

What the geometry genuinely does: R1 is one plane, 72 x 42 = 3,024 sf, 2.24x the 1,352 sf conditioned. roofJunctions computes 0. It covers every volume declared (main x12-56/y2-20, bay-w x-6-12, deck y-6-2, store y20-30, arrive x40-56/y20-32 all sit inside x-10..62, y-8..34). Refusing Harris's V is correct and is the best-argued line in the scheme: a valley down the middle of a 62 ft building at 3,400 ft is an ice dam, and this avoids it. The four give-backs are all real volumes, not prose: deck 496 sf, arrive 192 sf, store 280 sf, future bays 576 sf.

What the geometry does NOT do — the operation is "size the roof by the water it must collect," and the water does not appear anywhere in the volume list. There is no cistern volume, no berm, no leader. The only water number given is 2,500 gal, and it breaks the sizing argument three ways:

S7-DATUM.name: THE DATUM
S7-DATUM.critic: PARTLY — the disproportion is real in plan and fake in section. In plan the operation is delivered and is genuinely un-duplicated by the other seven: one declared roof plane, 80 x 48 = 3,840 sf, over a 44 x 22 = 968 sf conditioned footprint, 3.97:1, zero junctions, 17 piers, 19 CY. Nothing else in the set makes a canopy vastly larger than the house. But the operation's actual claim is "permanently dry hillside," and in section that claim is false. Computed roof underside runs 28.17 ft at the eave (y=-14) to 36.17 ft at the ridge (y=34); natural grade under it runs -4.86 to 15.94 ft. Clear height is 20.2 to 33.0 ft everywhere. Declared overhangs are 2 ft west, 2 ft east, 4 ft north, 6 ft south. Wind-driven rain off a 26 ft soffit at 30 degrees from vertical reaches 15.0 ft horizontally; at 15 degrees it still reaches 7.0 ft. Every declared overhang is beaten by a factor of 2 to 7. Nothing under this datum is dry. Lucy Carpet House's roof is ~10 ft above the ground it shelters; this is three times that, and the transferable thing about a sheltering datum is precisely its proximity, not its area. S7-ASSEMBLY.name: THE LOOP
S7-ASSEMBLY.critic:
Partly — the diagram embodies it, the arithmetic does not. Evidence FOR: one roof plane, zero junctions (the only scheme in the set that actually achieves the stated bar rather than approaching it); 36 lf of wet wall as the literal perimeter of one interior 8x10 block with the kitchen counter run on the block's west face at x=12, so no fixture touches an exterior wall; 15 CY of earth against hundreds for a bench; and growth by dropping a plate inside an enclosure that never changes (+100%, roof genuinely untouched). Those four are real and the discipline shows.

Evidence AGAINST, which is decisive: the headline object is "ONE closed rectangular loop, 104 lf, 52 identical 2 ft panels." The loop-s note then says "the whole 28 ft face is glass to -Y." 28 of 104 lf is 27% of the loop. The assembly is 76 lf and 38 panels, and the figure is a U, not a loop. The scheme's central number is contradicted by its own note two lines later.

Worse, the scheme simultaneously claims that wall is nothing ("nothing in here is structural") and that the roof and phase-2 floor span 24 ft in Y — which can only bear on y=2 and y=26. The y=2 wall must therefore carry both, and it is glass. A one-way solid

SX-SQUARE.name: THE SQUARE
SX-SQUARE.critic:
NO — the geometry does the opposite of what the operation claims, and the repo's own metric code proves it.

The operation is "a compact square maximises area against perimeter... be the squarest Henry can be." I rebuilt the scheme through model/schemes.mjs adopt()/metrics() at /home/user/henry-house/model/schemes.mjs. It scores perimeterLf 104, perimeterPerSf 0.077, conditionedSf 1352, shelteredSf 724 (0.536), wetWallLf 16, roofJunctions 0, cutCY 17, futureCapacityPct 46. It clears every bar. But unionPerimeter() rasterises the FOOTPRINT union, not built wall — so the metric measures storey count, not squareness. Decomposing the claimed 68 lf saving vs Sylvia (172 lf):
  1 storey at Sylvia's 1:3.1 aspect, 1352 sf: 171.2 lf (0.127)
  2 storeys at the SAME 1:3.1 aspect, 45.8 x 14.8: 121.1 lf (0.090) — already 29% inside the bar
  2 storeys square, 26 x 26: 104 lf (0.077)
Stacking buys 50.8 lf. Squaring buys 17.1 lf. Squareness is 25% of the operation; the second storey is 75%. And a one-storey 26x26 (676 sf, 104 lf) scores 0.154 — the square ALONE fails the 0.126 bar outright. The defining move cannot pass the test on its own.

S7-GROUND.name: THE WATERSHED
S7-GROUND.critic:
No. The operation is "landscape is part of the system — the house, its porch and the way water moves across the site are drawn as one thing." The vocabulary has exactly one slot for the ground, and this scheme spends it on `piers`. There is not one object in the geometry that is landscape. The interceptor swale, the level spreader, the gravel apron and the 5,000 gal cistern exist only in note strings. The one landscape item that was given a volume — `waterroom` — is declared kind:"shelt" with a single ffe of 0.5, i.e. a LEVEL platform, while its own note says "a gravel apron following natural grade, not a level platform." At ffe 0.5 across x8–32 / y-6–4 the declared pad cuts 2.7 ft at its NE corner and fills 2.2 ft at its SW (5.3 CY cut, 2.6 CY fill). The prose and the number disagree.

Where the water logic IS traceable in the numbers, the geometry inverts the thesis rather than serving it.

SX-STRATA.name: THE STRATA
SX-STRATA.critic:
NO — and the geometry proves it by a test the scheme cannot pass. THE OPERATION IS INVARIANT UNDER PERMUTATION OF BUILD ORDER. Swap the build sequence (second house first, then first house, shed last) and not one number in the file changes. Nothing in the geometry encodes WHICH object is older. The scheme asserts you read chronology in "the stepped eaves and the mismatched floor levels" — but I computed those levels against natural grade, and they are pure topography: first ffe 10.25 sits 0.31 ft over its max grade of 9.94; second 5.25 over 4.98 (+0.27); shed 12.25 over 12.04 (+0.21). Every level is a function of WHERE the object sits on a 30% cross-slope, not WHEN it was built. Three objects anywhere on this hill would step identically. The eaves likewise: R1 eave 27.75 ft, R2 23.25 ft — both derived by roofBase from ffe + storeys, i.e. from grade. Time leaves no trace.

The deeper contradiction is structural, not incidental. Longbranch is legible because the earlier cabin SURVIVES INSIDE the later work — the revelation IS the joint, the old exterior wall you can still touch from the new room.
